questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: What primarily motivated me to choose France was that I wanted to learn French. Furthermore, I knew that experiencing academic environments in other cultures could be a good experience to have, as it would offer new perspectives.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Paris because I wanted to learn French, and Paris was the only city that I had the option of going to. I chose Sorbonne Nouvelle specifically because they had an agreement with my department at the university, which I took to mean that they were specialized in cultural studies.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Sorbonne Nouvelle offered more information than the other Parisian universities that my housemates went to. They seemed to be more accustomed to welcoming foreign exchange students.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus coordinator was nice and answered any e-mail quite quickly, which was definitely a help.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I stayed at the Cité Universitaire. I can definitely recommend it. A really nice and multicultural environment, and the house that I stayed in had really good facilities. It was really nice to have housemates to talk to and have fun with.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's not really possible to live on-campus, but the university does offer housing through a bureau called Crous. These dorms are often a little better located than where I stayed, and I think it's nice to live in the same building as your classmates. The rent is also quite low, I think. On the other hand, the Crous-housing dormitories are very poorly managed. For example, the building of some of my friends was at one point flooded in the middle of the night, and they didn't really receive the necessary help to manage the situation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think you can definitely have a hard time finding housing in Paris, but if you apply either to Cité Universitaire or Crous, it should be fine.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The course registration process seemed to be easier at Sorbonne Nouvelle than at many other Parisian universities. But still, coming from University of Copenhagen where course registration is online and quite simple, the process seemed very old-fashioned and chaotic.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: In the first week, all the departments offered introductions to their courses and how to enroll in them. Every department had their own system, some used Google forms, others e-mail etc. As all the courses on bachelor level are 3 ECTS, it was a challenge to create a coherent schedule, as I had to take 10 different classes and make sure that they didn't overlap.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus coordinator was very helpful. Furthermore, the administration was nice.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember that if you register for back-to-back classes, that also means that you will have back-to-back midterms and exams.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Many of my courses were at an academic level that was equivalent to Danish high school. At the same time, though, the workload was very big. So I had a lot of work, but low academic outcome, which was frustrating. On the other hand, I guess it was alright that the academic level wasn't so high, since I was taking most of my courses in French, which I don't speak fluently.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style was more authoritarian. Some of my professors were nice enough, but others treated us students as children, ex. by scolding us if our classmates didn't show up for class. In some of my classes, oral participation was more about guessing what the teacher was thinking than doing any actual academic work. I found this very strange, as they taught humanities as if there was one true answer to a question. Furthermore, it was evident that the other students were not trained at all in doing independant academic work, which makes sense, as this was not encouraged at all.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Feel good littérature et development personnel, Cultures savantes et pop, Langues imaginaires et fiction, Littérature et jeunesse, Philosophie et science humaine, Creation divine d'homme, Politique britannique, Récits de la diaspora vietnamienne, Méthodologie et francais universitaire, Princesses dans la fiction

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Langues imaginaires et fiction was very interesting, the professor was good, the academic level was somewhat equivalent to a course at University of Copenhagen. Philosphie et science humaine was a course specifically for Erasmus students, so the level was very nice and the professor very professional and kind. Politique britannique was good because my professor was very competent, and the French style of teaching matched this field of studies better, where there actually is one correct answer to a question.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Prices on groceries are very high here - even higher than in Denmark, which was a surprise to me. Also, stuff like insurance, additional stuff for my room (duvet etc.) was surprisingly expensive. Also, you just spend more money on exchange than you normally would, when you have guests or go on day-trips.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries. Also, the French train system is punctual, but extremely expensive (outside of the city).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were a lot, but I didn't really use them.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Both sports and cultural activities such as cheap cinema tickets, theatre etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I went a lot to an event called "Lost in Frenchlation", which had nothing to do with the university, but was a really fun thing to do with other exchange students, as their concept is that they show French movies with English subtitles.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Going on daytrips is really nice, but train tickets can be expensive. Most museums are free for students, so that's nice. Also, just taking walks in the different neighborhoods is something I wish I'd done more. Going to get good food.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy. The culture isn't very different. I was frustrated, though, by the infrastructure of the city, that made me very dependent on the metro system.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The French students at my university were much nicer than I had anticipated. But you have to speak French, since most of them aren't comfortable speaking English.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching at the university. In Denmark, we students are treated as adults, and I feel that my Danish professors respect me. Here, it's very different.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People in public spaces were most of the time very kind and helpful. Also, Paris is a much more diverse city than Copenhagen, which is freeing and interesting.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: See if you can avoid having to take 30 ECTS in France, since that will (at least at Sorbonne Nouvelle) mean that you have to take 10 classes, which is just too much. If you aren't comfortable in French, try to take a few classes in English - it boosts your confidence to have a least a few classes where you can express yourself freely. If you're planning on taking only English classes, you should try to learn some French anyways, since it's very difficult to live or travel in France without speaking a basic level of French.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The professors try to tell you that attendance is mandatory, but it's not, really.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Improving my French level (although this as also been a straining process). Also, I've gotten a renewed appreciation for my home university (University of Copenhagen).

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Since I'm not fluent in French, I struggled with feeling out of place and a burden to the people I talked to. Also, I got really frustrated with my university, and I felt that I had too much work to enjoy my exchange.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Going on exchange to France is way more work than you normally imagine for an exchange semester. So you should really think it through before you choose to go.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
